obj.descent-lift.lift.formal: A \emph{lift} of the descent on $\nu$ modes is an isometry $W : H_{S} \to H_{S} \otimes H_{R}$, $H_{R}$ the Fock space of $k$ rungs, that is even, $W\G_{S} = (\G_{S}\otimes\G_{R})W$, and induces the descent on the even sector: the restriction of $W\rho W^{\dagger}$ to the system's algebra equals $\EN(\rho)$ for every even $\rho$. A lift is \emph{realised} by an even unitary $U$ on $H_{S}\otimes H_{R}$ with $W = U(\,\cdot \otimes \ket{0_{R}})$.
obj.descent-lift.lift.technical:
A lift of the descent on $\nu$ modes is an isometry $W: H_{S}\to H_{S}\otimes H_{R}$, with $H_{R}$ the Fock space of $k$ rungs, that is even, $W\G_{S} = (\G_{S}\otimes\G_{R})W$, and induces the descent on the even sector: the restriction of $W\rho W^{\dagger}$ to the system's algebra equals $\EN(\rho)$ for every even $\rho$.

A lift is realised by an even unitary $U$ on $H_{S}\otimes H_{R}$ when $W = U(\,\cdot\otimes\ket{0_{R}})$, that is, when it is produced by an evolution acting on the system with the record starting in its vacuum.
obj.descent-lift.lift.lay: A lift is a reversible way of carrying out the descent: instead of discarding information, it embeds the system in a larger space with extra record modes, so that the system on its own looks exactly as the descent leaves it. It must respect fermion parity, and it is called realised when an actual parity-respecting evolution, starting from an empty record, produces it.

obj.singularity.grading-parity-automorph.formal: Write $\Aa$ for the algebra generated by the completed pair, $\Aa \cong \Mat_2(\C)$ as a factor. It carries the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ grading it inherits from the Clifford algebra: $\Aev := \operatorname{span}\{1, \sigma\}$ is the even part and $\Aod := \operatorname{span}\{v, v^{*}\}$ the odd part, where $\sigma := v^{*}v - vv^{*}$ is the bivector of Theorem \claimref{singularity.modular-structure-completed-pair}. The \emph{parity automorphism} is $\alpha(x) := \sigma x \sigma$, well defined because $\sigma^{2} = 1$; it fixes $\Aev$ pointwise and acts by $-1$ on $\Aod$. On the full boundary mode space the parity automorphism is $\operatorname{Ad}(\Gamma)$ with $\Gamma := \prod_k \sigma_k$, the total fermion parity; the mode-wise refinement, one parity automorphism $\operatorname{Ad}(\sigma_k)$ per point of $E$, is Proposition \claimref{singularity.p-reduced-metric-level-reading-many}'s task, and on two or more modes the two generate different averages.
obj.singularity.grading-parity-automorph.technical:
The algebra $\Aa \cong \Mat_2(\C)$ generated by a completed pair $(v, v^{*})$ inherits a $\Z_2$ grading from the Clifford algebra: the even part is $\Aev = \operatorname{span}\{1, \sigma\}$ and the odd part is $\Aod = \operatorname{span}\{v, v^{*}\}$, where $\sigma = v^{*}v - vv^{*}$. Because $\sigma^{2} = 1$, conjugation $\alpha(x) = \sigma x \sigma$ is an automorphism, the parity automorphism; it fixes $\Aev$ pointwise and multiplies $\Aod$ by $-1$.

On the full boundary mode space the parity automorphism is $\operatorname{Ad}(\Gamma)$ with $\Gamma = \prod_k \sigma_k$, the total fermion parity. The finer mode-wise version, one automorphism $\operatorname{Ad}(\sigma_k)$ for each point of $E$, is treated separately, and on two or more modes the two generate different averages.
obj.singularity.grading-parity-automorph.lay: A single fermionic mode, described by two-by-two matrices, splits naturally into an even part (the identity and the element that tells empty from occupied) and an odd part (the operators that create or remove the fermion). The parity automorphism leaves the even part alone and flips the sign of the odd part. For many modes the natural version flips the sign according to the total number of fermions; flipping mode by mode is a different, finer operation.

obj.singularity.multi-mode-descent.formal:
For $N$ completed pairs $(v_k, v_k^*)$ with commuting occupation projectors $P_k := v_k^* v_k$, and for each $\varepsilon \in \{0,1\}^N$ the joint occupation projector $\Pi_\varepsilon := \prod_k \bigl(\varepsilon_k P_k + (1 - \varepsilon_k)(1 - P_k)\bigr)$ (orthogonal, complete: $\sum_\varepsilon \Pi_\varepsilon = 1$), the \emph{multi-mode descent} is the pinching
\[
\EN(x) \;:=\; \sum_{\varepsilon \in \{0,1\}^N} \Pi_\varepsilon\, x\, \Pi_\varepsilon ,
\]
the composition of the mode-wise maps of Proposition \claimref{singularity.descent-what-it-erases}. In the joint number representation, $\EN$ retains every matrix element diagonal in the joint occupation basis and erases every off-diagonal one: complete dephasing in the joint number basis. Its kernel is spanned by the operators carrying at least one off-diagonal mode factor, which is precisely the sector in which inter-mode coherence lies; its range is the algebra of joint-number-diagonal operators, the classical algebra of occupation records. That this range, and not the larger total-parity-even algebra, is the metric level on many modes is not a consequence of the grading: it is the composite argument of Proposition \claimref{singularity.p-reduced-metric-level-reading-many}, stated at the end of this step, where its effect is visible. One word of disambiguation, on which everything depends: ``pair'' here means one completed ladder pair, one \emph{mode}, in Rule 1's sense; the ``pairs'' of the section “The finite-mode model: the dissolution step by step”'s model are Hawking pairs, each two modes, one radiation and one window, so the model's $n$ pairs are $2n$ modes and $\EN$ there pinches all $2n$, one $\sigma_k$ per mode and never one per Hawking pair (on that wrong reading $\sigma$ would be the pair parity $\sigma_{R_k}\sigma_{L_k}$ ($Z_{R_k}Z_{L_k}$ in qubit notation, $Z = 1 - 2N = -\sigma$), the strictness witness would fail, and the deficit would be exactly zero).
obj.singularity.multi-mode-descent.technical:
For $N$ completed pairs with commuting occupation projectors $P_k = v_k^{*}v_k$, the joint occupation projectors $\Pi_\varepsilon$, $\varepsilon \in \{0,1\}^N$, are orthogonal and sum to the identity. The multi-mode descent is the pinching $\EN(x) = \sum_\varepsilon \Pi_\varepsilon\, x\, \Pi_\varepsilon$, the composite of the single-mode descents. In the joint number basis it keeps every diagonal matrix element and erases every off-diagonal one: its kernel is spanned by the operators with at least one off-diagonal mode factor, which is where inter-mode coherence lies, and its range is the algebra of joint-number-diagonal operators.

That this range, rather than the larger algebra that is even under total parity, is the metric level on many modes is not a consequence of the grading; it is argued separately. Here a "pair" means one completed ladder pair, that is one mode: a Hawking pair is two modes, and $\EN$ pinches each of them separately.
obj.singularity.multi-mode-descent.lay: With many fermionic modes, the multi-mode descent keeps only the record of which modes are occupied and discards every quantum coherence, including coherence between different modes. What survives is a classical list of occupation records. A Hawking pair counts as two modes here, and each is treated on its own.

obj.singularity.two-fibres-two-assemblie.formal: For $x \in E$ the \emph{small fibre} is the even part of the mode factor, $\Aa_x^{+} := \{a \in \Aa_x : \alpha_x(a) = a\} = \operatorname{span}\{1, \sigma(x)\}$, and the \emph{even subbundle} $\Aa^{+} \subseteq \Aa$ has these fibres. On a finite truncation $F = \{x_1, \dots, x_N\} \subseteq E$ with its $F$-mode algebra, the \emph{big fibre} at $x_j$ is $B_j := \operatorname{Fix}(\operatorname{Ad}\sigma(x_j))$, the elements of the whole $F$-mode algebra even in mode $j$, of dimension $4^N/2$; the small fibre lies inside it as the elements of mode $j$'s own factor. The \emph{sheaf assembly} is $\mathfrak{M}(U) := \Gamma(U, \Aa^{+})$ for open $U \subseteq E$, families $s$ with $s(x) \in \Aa_x^{+}$ at every $x \in U$, with the restriction maps of sections. The \emph{net assembly} is $J(F) :=$ the algebra generated in the $F$-mode algebra by $\bigcup_j B_j$, for finite $F$, with the inclusion maps $J(F) \hookrightarrow J(F')$ for $F \subseteq F'$.
obj.singularity.two-fibres-two-assemblie.technical:
At each point $x \in E$ the small fibre is the even part $\Aa_x^{+} = \operatorname{span}\{1, \sigma(x)\}$ of the mode factor, the elements fixed by the parity automorphism $\alpha_x$; together these form the even subbundle $\Aa^{+}$. On a finite truncation $F = \{x_1, \dots, x_N\}$ the big fibre at $x_j$ is $B_j = \operatorname{Fix}(\operatorname{Ad}\sigma(x_j))$, the elements of the whole $F$-mode algebra that are even in mode $j$, of dimension $4^N/2$; the small fibre sits inside it as the even part of mode $j$'s own factor.

Two assemblies of these pointwise levels are defined. The sheaf assembly is $\mathfrak{M}(U) = \Gamma(U, \Aa^{+})$, the sections of the even subbundle over open $U \subseteq E$ with the usual restriction maps. The net assembly $J(F)$ is the algebra generated by all the big fibres $B_j$ over finite $F$, with the inclusions $J(F) \hookrightarrow J(F')$ for $F \subseteq F'$.
obj.singularity.two-fibres-two-assemblie.lay: At each point of the singular locus there is one fermionic mode, and its parity-even part is a small two-dimensional algebra, the small fibre. When finitely many points are taken together, one can instead take everything in the combined system that is even in one chosen mode, the big fibre. The definition sets up two ways of gluing such pointwise pieces: as a sheaf of local sections of the small fibres, and as a net of algebras generated by the big fibres that grows with the set of points.

one-relation.imported-flag-arrow-superse.formal: The descent plants one Witt flag on the three-pair structure, a choice of half of each pair, whose single orientation bit is at once the arrow of time and the particle-antiparticle orientation. That this bit is initial data is a CPT-covariance argument the dark-matter paper states under three premises, the third of which, the exhaustiveness of its trichotomy, the corrected argument does not use. It rests on three premises: that CPT conjugation, an antilinear conjugation, is an isomorphism of every kinematic structure and leaves every action functional invariant, the gauge couplings included (premised for the derived gauge sector); Hypothesis (S), the Standard-Model paper's open premise that the composite's slots carry fermionic statistics; and the premise that the flag is a datum of each solution, planted by the descent, rather than part of the kinematic structure. Its last step reaches initial data directly, as a conjugation-odd bit on conjugation-stable solution spaces, which excludes a parameter of the laws without any exhaustiveness. The flag is a $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ datum, an orientation, and not a choice of frame vector. That the framework inherits its asymmetry rather than generating it, with two unexplained continuous numbers, is a declared stance there and is carried as one here. Tower charge is superselected exactly, making sectors mutually dark rather than mutually exclusive. \emph{Provenance:} \cite[Def.~2.10, Prop.~4.1, Prop.~5.1 (stance), Prop.~5.2 (stated under three premises; the corrected argument replaces the exhaustiveness premise by the flag as a datum)]{ButlerT14}; Hypothesis (S) is declared in \cite[\S5]{ButlerT12}.

scrambling.imported-modes-modular-invent.formal: For a completed pair, the boost bivector $\sigma$ satisfies $\sigma^2 = 1$, generates the rotor flow with weights $\mp 1$ on the pair, has the occupation projectors as spectral projectors, acts in Fock representation through $\tfrac12\sigma = N - \tfrac12$, and is the unique one-parameter rotor flow of the atom \emph{up to reparametrisation of the flow parameter and orientation} (the bivector space is one-dimensional: the algebra fixes the orbits, not the speed, which is the normalisation the geometry supplies). The geometric normalisation converts rapidity to Schwarzschild time at the surface gravity $\kappa = 1/4M$. Continued to imaginary rapidity, the boost rotor becomes a unitary of the complexified atom whose conjugation action has period exactly $2\pi$; the continuation's generator $I_{5}\sigma$, with $I_{5} = I_{4}e$ the central pseudoscalar of the odd extension $\Cl(2,3)$, the unit of the continued rotor acting on spacetime vectors (the $(\varrho, \tau)$ plane, \claimref{std-algebra.complexification-is-the-odd-extension}), lies outside the real algebra $\Cl(1,3)$, so the cycle belongs to the clock's Euclidean continuation, not to any intrinsic flow of the boundary modes. On the atom's own modes the complex unit is $J = e_{2}e_{3}$ (\claimref{synthesis.transverse-bivector-is-the-complex-unit-of-the-radial-atom}), and the continued flow there is conjugation by $e^{I_{4}\theta/2}$, a different object. \emph{Provenance:} \cite[Prop.~2.1]{ButlerT7} (proved self-contained there); the normalisation \cite[App.~A]{ButlerT5}; the continuation and its $2\pi$ conjugation period \cite[Prop.~7.21(1)]{ButlerT5}; the exclusion of $I_{5}\sigma$ from the real algebra \cite[Prop.~7.21(3)]{ButlerT5}.
scrambling.imported-modes-modular-invent.technical:
For a completed pair, the boost bivector $\sigma = v^{*}v - vv^{*}$ satisfies $\sigma^{2} = 1$, generates the rotor flow under which the two ladder elements carry weights $\mp 1$, has the occupation projectors as its spectral projectors, and in the Fock representation satisfies $\tfrac12\sigma = N - \tfrac12$. It is the unique one-parameter rotor flow of the atom up to reparametrisation of the flow parameter and orientation: the bivector space is one-dimensional, so the algebra fixes the orbits but not the speed, and the geometric normalisation converts rapidity to Schwarzschild time at surface gravity $\kappa = 1/4M$.

Continued to imaginary rapidity, the boost rotor becomes a unitary of the complexified atom whose conjugation action has period exactly $2\pi$. Its generator $I_{5}\sigma$, $I_{5} = I_{4}e$ the central unit of $\Cl(2,3)$ for the continued rotor acting on spacetime vectors, lies outside the real algebra $\Cl(1,3)$, so this cycle belongs to the clock's Euclidean continuation and not to any intrinsic flow of the boundary modes.
scrambling.imported-modes-modular-invent.lay: Each boundary mode carries a built-in clock: one element that generates boosts, counts whether the mode is occupied, and supplies the projections used to discard coherence. The algebra fixes the shape of this clock's motion but not its rate; the black hole's geometry sets the rate through its surface gravity. Continuing the clock to imaginary time gives a cycle of period $2\pi$, but that cycle lies outside the real algebra, so it is not a genuine motion of the modes.

scrambling.imported-time-plane-modular-d.formal: The modular flow of a wedge algebra in the vacuum implements the boost: the timelike direction is recoverable from modular data (Bisognano-Wichmann). One half-sided modular inclusion recovers the two-dimensional conformal structure (Wiesbrock). \emph{Provenance:} \cite{BisognanoWichmann1976} (the duality theorem) and \cite{Wiesbrock1993} (the main theorem); both at assembly level for the present use.
scrambling.imported-time-plane-modular-d.technical: For the algebra of a wedge in the vacuum, the modular flow implements the boost that preserves the wedge (Bisognano and Wichmann), so the timelike direction can be recovered from modular data alone. A single half-sided modular inclusion of von Neumann algebras recovers the two-dimensional conformal structure (Wiesbrock). Both results are used here at the level of the assembled algebras.
scrambling.imported-time-plane-modular-d.lay: In quantum field theory, the vacuum restricted to a wedge-shaped region of spacetime comes with an intrinsic time evolution, and a classic theorem shows that it is exactly the boost preserving the wedge. So the direction of time can be read off from the algebra and the state alone. A related theorem recovers the whole two-dimensional plane of time and one space direction from a particular nesting of two algebras.

imported_from.citation: J. J. Bisognano and E. H. Wichmann, On the duality condition for quantum fields, J. Math. Phys. 17 (1976), 303--321.

singularity.ascended-marginals-are-diago.formal: Let $\omega$ satisfy (P). Then $\omega(v_k) = \omega(v_k^{*}) = 0$ at every mode, so the ascended marginal $\varrho_k$ is diagonal in the number basis, coincides with $E_k(\varrho_k)$, and is by Theorem \claimref{singularity.descended-form-state-independent} the Gibbs state of $K_k$ at a unique $\beta_k$ for $\omega_k \neq 0$ (at a zero-weight mode diagonality still holds, and the Gibbs form requires $p_k = \tfrac12$, Theorem \claimref{singularity.descended-form-state-independent}'s parenthesis). Consequently partial trace and pinching coincide on every single-mode marginal, which is Proposition \claimref{singularity.pinching-against-partial-trace-scope-coincidence}(i) with hypothesis (ii) of Theorem \claimref{singularity.modular-descent} removed; and the parity protection lemma of the finite-mode model, Lemma \claimref{singularity.parity-protection}, is the special case of this theorem for the model's states, which are even because every configuration in their support has even total occupation.
singularity.ascended-marginals-are-diago.technical:
For a state $\omega$ satisfying univalence, $\omega \circ \alpha = \omega$, the odd ladder elements of each mode have vanishing expectation: $\omega(v_k) = \omega(\alpha(v_k)) = -\omega(v_k)$, so $\omega(v_k) = \omega(v_k^{*}) = 0$. These are exactly the off-diagonal entries of the single-mode marginal $\varrho_k$ in the number basis, so $\varrho_k$ is diagonal and equals $E_k(\varrho_k)$. By the state independence of the descended form it is then the Gibbs state of $K_k$ at a unique $\beta_k$ when $\omega_k \neq 0$; at a zero-weight mode diagonality still holds, but the Gibbs form requires $p_k = \tfrac12$.

Consequently partial trace and pinching coincide on every single-mode marginal of such a state, without the extra hypothesis that was needed before. The parity protection lemma of the finite-mode model is the special case of the model's states, which are even because every configuration in their support has even total occupation.
singularity.ascended-marginals-are-diago.lay: If the physical states of the boundary modes are required to be even under fermion parity (premise (P)), then each mode, looked at on its own, carries no coherence between being empty and being occupied. Its description reduces to a pair of probabilities. When the mode has nonzero weight, that pair is exactly a thermal distribution at a temperature of its own, so the thermal form of each single mode follows from parity rather than being assumed. That every mode shares the Hawking temperature needs a further premise and is not part of this result.

The off-diagonal entries of $\varrho_k$ in the number basis are exactly $\omega(v_k)$ and $\omega(v_k^{*})$, those being the mode's two off-diagonal matrix units. singularity.chains-state-class-stability.technical:
Let $\mathcal{C}$ be the set of even states of the boundary modes all of whose single-mode marginals are the Gibbs state of $K_k$ at $\beta = 2\pi/\kappa$. Under premises (P) and (R) the state of the boundary modes lies in $\mathcal{C}$, and every member of $\mathcal{C}$ satisfies (P) and (R). Every internal dynamics that (L$_E$) permits is conjugation by a diagonal unitary, which commutes with the total parity and preserves every marginal, so $\mathcal{C}$ is invariant: a state placed in it at injection stays in it, whatever the boundary modes write.

The class contains the product state $e^{-\beta K_{\mathrm{geo}}}/Z$, its only member satisfying (G), and also states of arbitrarily large total correlation $C(\varrho)$ and descent deficit; (R) constrains none of the correlations. So under these premises the marginals are fixed once and for all, while the joint state is left free.

singularity.descended-form-state-indepen.formal:
Let $\varrho$ be the density matrix of \emph{any} state on the boundary mode space, and $\varrho_k$ its marginal at mode $k$. Then $E_k(\varrho_k)$ is diagonal in that mode's number basis, and therefore
\[
E_k(\varrho_k) \;=\; \frac{e^{-\beta_k \omega_k N_k}}{Z_k}
\]
for a unique $\beta_k \in [-\infty, +\infty]$, determined by $\beta_k\omega_k = \log\bigl(p_k/(1-p_k)\bigr)$ with $p_k$ the descended vacancy probability. (Stated for $\omega_k \neq 0$: at a zero-weight mode the right side is $\tfrac12\,\mathrm{id}$ for every $\beta_k$, so uniqueness always fails there, and existence fails unless $p_k = \tfrac12$.) The descended single-mode state is a Gibbs state of the boost generator $K_k$ whatever the ascended state was: no hypothesis on the state is used.
singularity.descended-form-state-indepen.technical:
For any state on the boundary mode space and any mode $k$, the descended marginal $E_k(\varrho_k)$ is diagonal in the number basis, because the range of $E_k$ is the even subalgebra. A diagonal density matrix $\operatorname{diag}(p_k, 1 - p_k)$ is then the Gibbs state $e^{-\beta_k\omega_k N_k}/Z_k$ for a unique $\beta_k \in [-\infty, +\infty]$, fixed by $\beta_k\omega_k = \log\bigl(p_k/(1-p_k)\bigr)$, provided $\omega_k \neq 0$.

At a zero-weight mode the right side is $\tfrac12\,\id$ for every $\beta_k$, so uniqueness fails there and existence requires $p_k = \tfrac12$. No hypothesis on the ascended state is used.
singularity.descended-form-state-indepen.lay: Once the descent has removed a mode's coherences, what remains is just the probability of the mode being empty or occupied. Any such pair of probabilities can be read as a thermal state at exactly one temperature, allowing the extreme cases at either end. This holds whatever state the system started in, provided the mode has nonzero weight.

proofs.main: By Theorem \claimref{singularity.descent-parity-average} the range of $E_k$ is the even subalgebra, which in the number basis is the diagonal. A diagonal density matrix on a two-dimensional space is $\operatorname{diag}(p_k, 1 - p_k)$, and $\beta_k \mapsto (1 + e^{\beta_k\omega_k})^{-1}$ is a bijection from $\R$ onto $(0,1)$, so every such matrix with $0 < p_k < 1$ is the stated Gibbs matrix for exactly one $\beta_k$; the two boundary values are the limits $\beta_k = \pm\infty$.

singularity.descent-parity-average.formal:
For every $x \in \Aa$,
\[
E(x) \;=\; \tfrac12\bigl(x + \alpha(x)\bigr) \;=\; \tfrac12\bigl(x + \sigma x \sigma\bigr) .
\]
Consequently $E$ is the group average over $\{\id, \alpha\}$, hence the unique conditional expectation of $\Aa$ onto its fixed-point algebra $\Aev$; its range is $\Aev$ and its kernel is exactly $\Aod$, the adjoined ladder sector; and $E$ preserves every state $\omega$ with $\omega \circ \alpha = \omega$.
singularity.descent-parity-average.technical:
On the single-mode algebra $\Aa$ the descent equals the parity average: $E(x) = \tfrac12\bigl(x + \alpha(x)\bigr) = \tfrac12(x + \sigma x \sigma)$. Hence $E$ is the group average over $\{\id, \alpha\}$ and the unique conditional expectation of $\Aa$ onto its fixed-point algebra $\Aev$.

Its range is $\Aev$, its kernel is exactly the adjoined ladder sector $\Aod$, and it preserves every state with $\omega \circ \alpha = \omega$.
singularity.descent-parity-average.lay: The descent, which keeps a mode's occupation data and discards its coherences, is the same thing as averaging over fermion parity: take an observable and its parity-flipped version and average the two. This makes it the only consistent projection onto the parity-even observables, and it leaves every parity-even state unchanged.

proofs.main:
Write $x = a\,vv^{*} + b\,v + c\,v^{*} + d\,v^{*}v$ as in Proposition \claimref{singularity.descent-what-it-erases}, with $P = v^{*}v$ and $\sigma = 2P - 1 = v^{*}v - vv^{*}$. By the CAR and $v^{2} = (v^{*})^{2} = 0$, $\sigma$ commutes with $vv^{*}$ and $v^{*}v$ and anticommutes with $v$ and $v^{*}$ ($\sigma v = -v = -v\sigma$, $\sigma v^{*} = v^{*} = -v^{*}\sigma$), and $\sigma^{2} = 1$; then
\[
\alpha(x) = \sigma x \sigma = a\,vv^{*} - b\,v - c\,v^{*} + d\,v^{*}v ,
\]
so $\tfrac12(x + \alpha(x)) = a\,vv^{*} + d\,v^{*}v$, which is the value of $E$ computed in Proposition \claimref{singularity.descent-what-it-erases}. (In the defining representation, a labelled reading, $v = E_{12}$, $v^{*} = E_{21}$, $\sigma = \operatorname{diag}(-1, +1)$, and $\alpha$ flips the signs of the off-diagonal entries.) The average of a finite group acting by automorphisms is a conditional expectation onto the fixed-point algebra. It is moreover the unique conditional expectation of $\Aa$ onto $\Aev$, by bimodularity: if $F$ is any conditional expectation onto $\Aev$, then for odd $x$, since $\sigma \in \Aev$ and $\sigma x \sigma = -x$, bimodularity gives $\sigma F(x) \sigma = F(\sigma x \sigma) = -F(x)$, while $F(x) \in \Aev$ is fixed by conjugation with $\sigma$, so $F(x) = -F(x) = 0$: every conditional expectation onto $\Aev$ annihilates the $(-1)$-eigenspace of $\alpha$, which is $\Aod = \operatorname{span}\{v, v^{*}\}$, and agrees with the identity on $\Aev$, hence equals $E$ on $\Aa = \Aev \oplus \Aod$. State preservation is $\omega(E(x)) = \tfrac12(\omega(x) + \omega(\alpha(x))) = \omega(x)$. The script verifies the identity, idempotence, the conditional-expectation property $E(axb) = aE(x)b$ for even $a, b$, and the range and kernel, on generic rational data.

singularity.descent-what-it-erases.formal:
Set $P := v^* v$. Then $P^2 = P$, $1 - P = v v^*$, and every element of the mode algebra is $x = a\,vv^{*} + b\,v + c\,v^{*} + d\,v^{*}v$ for unique scalars $a, b, c, d$. With
\[
E(x) := P x P + (1{-}P)\,x\,(1{-}P), \qquad
E\bigl(a\,vv^{*} + b\,v + c\,v^{*} + d\,v^{*}v\bigr) = a\,vv^{*} + d\,v^{*}v .
\]
Descent retains the occupation data $a, d$ and erases the coherences $b, c$. (In the defining $2 \times 2$ representation, a labelled reading, $v = E_{12}$, $v^{*} = E_{21}$, $vv^{*} = E_{11}$, $P = E_{22} = \operatorname{diag}(0, 1)$, and $E$ sends the matrix with entries $a, b, c, d$ to $\operatorname{diag}(a, d)$.)
singularity.descent-what-it-erases.technical:
With $P := v^* v$, the anticommutation relation and $v^2 = (v^*)^2 = 0$ give $P^2 = P$ and $1 - P = v v^*$. Every element of the mode algebra is $x = a\,vv^{*} + b\,v + c\,v^{*} + d\,v^{*}v$.

The descent $E(x) := PxP + (1-P)\,x\,(1-P)$ sends $x$ to $a\,vv^{*} + d\,v^{*}v$: it retains the occupation data and erases the coherences $b, c$. In the defining $2 \times 2$ representation ($v = E_{12}$, $v^* = E_{21}$, $P = \operatorname{diag}(0,1)$) it keeps the diagonal of the matrix with entries $a, b, c, d$.
singularity.descent-what-it-erases.lay: A single fermionic mode can be described by a two-by-two matrix. The descent keeps the two diagonal entries, which record whether the mode is empty or occupied, and discards the two off-diagonal entries, which record quantum coherence between those two possibilities.

singularity.finite-truncation-meet-big-f.formal:
For finite $F = \{x_1, \dots, x_N\} \subseteq E$,
\[
\bigcap_{j} B_j \;=\; \Bigl\langle \bigcup_j \Aa_{x_j}^{+} \Bigr\rangle \;=\; \operatorname{range}(E_F),
\]
the joint-number-diagonal algebra, of dimension $2^N$: the meet of the big fibres and the join of the small fibres coincide, and both are the algebra of compatible evaluations of $\mathfrak{M}$ at the points of $F$. Here $\langle\,\cdot\,\rangle$ denotes the generated subalgebra.
singularity.finite-truncation-meet-big-f.technical:
On a finite truncation $F = \{x_1, \dots, x_N\} \subseteq E$, three algebras coincide: the meet $\bigcap_j B_j$ of the big fibres, the subalgebra generated by the small fibres $\Aa_{x_j}^{+}$, and the range of the multi-mode descent $E_F$. All three are the joint-number-diagonal algebra, of dimension $2^N$, and this is also the algebra of compatible evaluations of the sheaf assembly $\mathfrak{M}$ at the points of $F$.

The meet is the joint-diagonal algebra because, by the mode-wise parity proposition, an element fixed by every $\operatorname{Ad}\sigma(x_j)$ is diagonal in the joint number basis and conversely. The join reaches the same algebra because the commuting single-site $\sigma(x_j)$ generate the $2^N$ independent diagonal monomials $\prod_{j \in S}\sigma(x_j)$, $S \subseteq F$.
singularity.finite-truncation-meet-big-f.lay: On finitely many modes there are two natural ways to build the algebra of classical occupation records: keep only what is even in every mode separately, or combine the even parts of the individual modes. This result shows that the two give the same algebra, which is also exactly what the multi-mode descent keeps. It has dimension two to the power of the number of modes, one dimension for each pattern of occupations.

The join: the $\sigma(x_j)$ commute, are single-site in the Jordan-Wigner representation (the strings cancel in $v^{*}v - vv^{*}$), and generate the $2^N$ independent monomials $\prod_{j \in S}\sigma(x_j)$, $S \subseteq F$, each joint-diagonal; so the join is a subalgebra of the meet of the same dimension. Compatible evaluations of $\mathfrak{M}$ at the points of $F$ are exactly tuples in $\prod_j \Aa_{x_j}^{+}$ (every tuple occurs, by bump functions), and the algebra they generate is the join.

singularity.imported-descent-one-way-con.formal: $E$ is a conditional expectation onto the commutant of $P$, its kernel is exactly the adjoined ladder sector, and no unital algebra homomorphism from the completed algebra back to its base exists at all: ascent is two-way for what was lifted from the original space, one-way for what was built in the completion. It is moreover the unique conditional expectation onto that subalgebra preserving the trace. \emph{Provenance:} the conditional expectation property, the kernel and the non-existence of a return homomorphism are \cite[Prop.~7.5, Thm.~7.6]{ButlerT1}; the uniqueness of the trace-preserving conditional expectation onto a von Neumann subalgebra is Takesaki's theorem \cite{Takesaki1972}, and in the present order-two case it is also Theorem \claimref{singularity.descent-parity-average}.
singularity.imported-descent-one-way-con.technical:
The descent $E$ is a conditional expectation onto the commutant of the occupation projector $P$, and its kernel is exactly the adjoined ladder sector. No unital algebra homomorphism from the completed algebra back to its base exists at all: ascent is two-way for what was lifted from the original space and one-way for what was built in the completion.

Moreover $E$ is the unique trace-preserving conditional expectation onto that subalgebra. This is Takesaki's theorem on conditional expectations onto von Neumann subalgebras, and in the present order-two case it also follows from the identification of $E$ with the parity average.
singularity.imported-descent-one-way-con.lay: Stepping down from the enlarged algebra to the original one is a well-behaved averaging projection that keeps the occupation data and discards exactly the newly added ladder sector. There is no way back: what was built only in the enlarged algebra cannot be returned to the original by any structure-preserving map. Among such projections that preserve the trace, it is the only one.

singularity.imported-general-form.formal: For a $C^{*}$-dynamical system the $(\alpha,\beta)$-KMS states at fixed $\beta$ form a weak$^{*}$-compact convex simplex whose extreme points are exactly those whose GNS von Neumann algebra is a factor, distinct extremal KMS states being disjoint; a factor state is therefore extremal, and uniqueness at fixed $\beta$ is the statement that the simplex is a point. \emph{Provenance:} Bratteli and Robinson \cite[Thm.~5.3.30]{BR2}, the KMS condition itself being \cite{HHW1967}. The companion statement that two faithful normal states with the same modular automorphism group differ by an element affiliated to the centre, hence coincide on a factor, is Connes' Radon-Nikodym cocycle theorem \cite[Thm.~1.2.1]{Connes1973}.
singularity.imported-general-form.technical:
For a $C^{*}$-dynamical system the $(\alpha,\beta)$-KMS states at fixed $\beta$ form a weak$^{*}$-compact convex simplex. Its extreme points are exactly the KMS states whose GNS von Neumann algebra is a factor, and distinct extremal KMS states are disjoint; so a factor state is extremal, and uniqueness of the KMS state at fixed $\beta$ is the statement that the simplex is a single point.

The companion statement is Connes' Radon-Nikodym cocycle theorem: two faithful normal states with the same modular automorphism group differ by an element affiliated to the centre, and hence coincide on a factor.
singularity.imported-general-form.lay: The equilibrium states of a quantum system at a given temperature form a convex set, and its corners are the states that cannot be split into simpler equilibria. These corners are exactly the states whose associated algebra has a trivial centre. A related theorem says that on such an algebra a faithful state is determined by its intrinsic time evolution.

singularity.imported-univalence-supersel.formal: In a theory whose field algebra is $\mathbb{Z}_2$ graded by fermion number, coherent superpositions of states of opposite fermion parity are not observable: the observable algebra is the even subalgebra and physical states are even. \emph{Provenance:} Wick, Wightman and Wigner \cite{WWW1952}; the graded structure of CAR algebras and their even subalgebras is \cite[\S 5.2]{BR2}. What the rule superselects is the total parity, a single $\mathbb{Z}_2$; the mode-wise strengthening that the multi-mode descent of Step 5 needs is Proposition \claimref{singularity.p-reduced-metric-level-reading-many}, stated there, and is not part of this import.
singularity.imported-univalence-supersel.technical: In a theory whose field algebra is $\Z_2$ graded by fermion number, coherent superpositions of states of opposite fermion parity are not observable: the observable algebra is the even subalgebra and physical states are even (Wick, Wightman and Wigner, with the graded structure of CAR algebras and their even subalgebras from the standard literature). The rule superselects only the total parity, a single $\Z_2$; the mode-wise strengthening that the multi-mode descent needs is a separate statement and not part of this import.
singularity.imported-univalence-supersel.lay: A classic rule of quantum theory says that one can never observe a superposition of a state with an even number of fermions and one with an odd number. So the observable quantities are those unchanged by flipping fermion parity, and physical states respect this. The rule concerns the total count of fermions only, not each mode separately.

imported_from.citation: G. C. Wick, A. S. Wightman and E. P. Wigner, The intrinsic parity of elementary particles, Phys. Rev. 88 (1952), 101--105.

singularity.kms-uniqueness-factor.formal: Let $\Aa$ be a matrix factor, with scalars $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_4\}$ (the default scalar field of an abstract complex matrix algebra), $\alpha_t = \operatorname{Ad}(e^{I_4tK})$ a flow and $\beta \neq 0$. A state $\omega = \tr(\varrho\,\cdot\,)$ is $(\alpha,\beta)$-KMS if and only if $\varrho = e^{-\beta K}/\tr e^{-\beta K}$. In particular there is exactly one KMS state for each $\beta$, and, for $K$ not a multiple of $1$, the KMS states of the flow form a line parametrised by $\beta$.
singularity.kms-uniqueness-factor.technical:
On a matrix factor $\Aa$ over $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_4\}$ with the inner flow $\alpha_t = \operatorname{Ad}(e^{I_4tK})$ and any $\beta \neq 0$, a state $\omega = \tr(\varrho\,\cdot\,)$ satisfies the $(\alpha,\beta)$-KMS condition exactly when $\varrho = e^{-\beta K}/\tr e^{-\beta K}$. Writing the KMS identity $\omega(ab) = \omega(b\,e^{-\beta K}a\,e^{\beta K})$ as traces and using cyclicity shows that $\varrho\,e^{\beta K}$ commutes with every element, so it is central and therefore scalar because the algebra is a factor; normalisation fixes the constant, and the converse is the same computation read backwards.

So for each nonzero $\beta$ there is exactly one KMS state, and, for $K$ not a multiple of $1$, the KMS states of the flow form a single line parametrised by $\beta$.
singularity.kms-uniqueness-factor.lay: In a finite quantum system described by a full matrix algebra, a time evolution generated by an operator K singles out equilibrium states, one for each temperature. This result shows that for each nonzero inverse temperature there is exactly one such state, and it is the familiar Gibbs (Boltzmann) state built from K. Unless K is a multiple of the identity (when every temperature gives the same state), the equilibrium states therefore form a single family labelled by temperature.

proofs.main:
In finite dimensions the KMS condition reads $\omega(ab) = \omega\bigl(b\,\alpha_{I_4\beta}(a)\bigr) = \omega\bigl(b\,e^{-\beta K}a\,e^{\beta K}\bigr)$ for all $a, b$. Writing both sides as traces and using cyclicity, the left side is $\tr(b\varrho a)$ and the right side is $\tr\bigl(e^{\beta K}\varrho\, b\, e^{-\beta K} a\bigr)$, so for all $b$,
\[
b\,\bigl(\varrho\, e^{\beta K}\bigr) \;=\; \bigl(e^{\beta K}\varrho\bigr)\, b .
\]
Taking $b = 1$ gives $\varrho e^{\beta K} = e^{\beta K}\varrho$, so $\varrho$ commutes with $K$; the displayed identity then says that $\varrho\,e^{\beta K}$ commutes with everything, hence is central, hence scalar because $\Aa$ is a factor. So $\varrho \propto e^{-\beta K}$, and normalisation fixes the constant. The converse is the same computation read backwards. The script checks the identity on all sixteen matrix-unit pairs for $\varrho \propto \operatorname{diag}(1, \tfrac{16}{9})$ and exhibits a pair at which the tracial state fails it.

singularity.modular-descent.formal:
Let the ascended algebra of the horizon pair carry any state that is (i) pure, (ii) invariant under the boost flow generated by $\sigma$, and (iii) entangling across the two ends of the pair (cyclic and separating for the one-sided subalgebra). Then the descended state, the partial trace over the partner, which for such a state coincides with the restriction under the pinching $E$ of Proposition \claimref{singularity.descent-what-it-erases} (Proposition \claimref{singularity.pinching-against-partial-trace-scope-coincidence}(i); the coincidence is exactly single-mode, Proposition \claimref{singularity.pinching-against-partial-trace-scope-coincidence}(ii)), is KMS for the phase flow $\operatorname{Ad}(e^{Jt\sigma/2})$ of $\sigma$, $J = e_{2}e_{3}$ the complex unit of the atom (\claimref{synthesis.transverse-bivector-is-the-complex-unit-of-the-radial-atom}), at some inverse temperature $\beta \in \R$ in rapidity, and the hypotheses leave $\beta$ free, its sign included: nothing in (i) to (iii) forces $\beta > 0$ (the descended form of Theorem \claimref{singularity.descended-form-state-independent} allows the closed range $[-\infty, +\infty]$, and hypothesis (iii) removes exactly the endpoints), and positivity arrives with (R). If the modular parameter is normalised to the geometric period, one modular period being one period $2\pi/\kappa$ of rapidity-time (the Bisognano-Wichmann normalisation, which the section “What selects the state” names as premise (R) and proves irreducible), then $\beta = 2\pi$ in rapidity and, by Proposition \claimref{singularity.plane-rate}, the physical temperature is
\[
T \;=\; \frac{\kappa}{2\pi} \;=\; \frac{1}{8\pi M} \;=\; \TH ,
\]
exactly the Hawking temperature. For the CAR pair, the reduced density matrix per mode of frequency $\omega$ is then the Fermi-Dirac matrix $\operatorname{diag}(1, e^{-\omega/T})/Z$ with occupancy $1/(e^{\omega/T} + 1)$. The hypotheses are sufficient, not necessary: a state violating (ii) or (iii) need not descend thermally, and the projection cannot make it do so, but some such states do (the proof exhibits one), and Theorem \claimref{singularity.descended-form-state-independent} explains why no hypothesis on the state can be necessary for the \emph{form}.
singularity.modular-descent.technical:
Let the ascended algebra of the horizon pair carry a state that is (i) pure, (ii) invariant under the boost flow generated by $\sigma$, and (iii) entangling across the two ends of the pair, that is cyclic and separating for the one-sided subalgebra. Then the descended state, the partial trace over the partner, is KMS for the phase flow $\operatorname{Ad}(e^{Jt\sigma/2})$ of $\sigma$, $J = e_2e_3$ the atom's complex unit, at some inverse temperature $\beta \in \R$ in rapidity, and the hypotheses leave $\beta$ free, its sign included; positivity arrives only with (R).

Under the geometric normalisation (R), one modular period equal to one period $2\pi/\kappa$ of rapidity-time, one gets $\beta = 2\pi$ in rapidity, and the rapidity-to-time conversion gives the physical temperature $T = \kappa/2\pi = 1/8\pi M = \TH$. For the CAR pair the reduced density matrix of a mode of frequency $\omega$ is then the Fermi-Dirac matrix $\operatorname{diag}(1, e^{-\omega/T})/Z$. The hypotheses are sufficient, not necessary: some states violating (ii) or (iii) still descend thermally, and some do not.
singularity.modular-descent.lay: Suppose the quantum state of a horizon mode and its partner is pure, unchanged by the boost, and genuinely entangled across the pair. Then what is seen on one side is thermal, although these conditions alone do not fix the temperature, not even its sign. Adding the premise that ties the state's intrinsic time to the geometric period of the horizon gives exactly the Hawking temperature, with a Fermi-Dirac occupation for each mode. The conditions are enough for this conclusion but are not required for it.

proofs.main:
The pair algebra is the $2 \times 2$ factor generated by $(v, v^*)$; its commutant in the doubled system is the partner copy, and hypotheses (i) and (iii) say exactly that the state vector is cyclic and separating for the pair factor. By Lemma \claimref{singularity.schmidt-forcing-proved-outright}, hypothesis (ii) forces
\[
|\Omega\rangle = \cos\theta\,|00\rangle + \sin\theta\,|11\rangle, \qquad \cos\theta\sin\theta \neq 0 ,
\]
and by Lemma \claimref{singularity.modular-theory-matrix-factor-proved-outright} (with $n = 2$, $\lambda_0 = \cos\theta$, $\lambda_1 = \sin\theta$) the modular operator of $|\Omega\rangle$ is $\Delta = \rho \otimes \bar\rho^{\,-1}$ with $\rho = \operatorname{diag}(\cos^2\theta, \sin^2\theta)$ and modular flow $t \mapsto \operatorname{Ad}(\rho^{Jt})$ on the pair factor, KMS identity included (the Lemma, stated over $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_4\}$, read over the atom's scalars $\mathrm{span}\{1, J\}$, $J = e_2e_3$). So far the state is Gibbs for $K$ at an inverse temperature $\beta$ determined by $\tan^{2}\theta = e^{-\beta}$, and nothing in (i) to (iii) constrains $\theta$: this is the residue the section “What selects the state” takes up. It remains to normalise, and this one step is an import. Assign the mode its frequency by scaling the boost generator: the physical generator of the flow is $\omega K$, $K = N - \tfrac12$ (Theorem \claimref{singularity.modular-structure-completed-pair}(4)), and Proposition \claimref{singularity.plane-rate} converts rapidity to Schwarzschild time at rate $\kappa$. The modular group of Lemma \claimref{singularity.modular-theory-matrix-factor-proved-outright} runs at parameter $t$ with generator $\log\Delta$; demanding, by premise (R) (\claimref{singularity.r-regularity-fixed-locus}), that modular parameter $2\pi$ correspond to the geometric flow of $\omega K$ over one period $2\pi/\kappa$ of rapidity-time forces $\log\rho = -(2\pi/\kappa)\,\omega N + \text{const}$, i.e.
\[
\rho \;\propto\; e^{-(2\pi/\kappa)\,\omega N}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\tan\theta = e^{-\omega/2T}, \qquad T = \frac{\kappa}{2\pi} ,
\]
since $\rho = \operatorname{diag}(\cos^2\theta, \sin^2\theta)$ and $N = \operatorname{diag}(0,1)$. The partial trace over the partner is then $\rho_{\text{mode}} = \operatorname{diag}(1, e^{-\omega/T})/Z$: Fermi-Dirac at exactly $\TH$, manifestly KMS for the flow of $K$ by the last clause of Lemma \claimref{singularity.modular-theory-matrix-factor-proved-outright}. What the hypotheses do and do not force: if (ii) fails, Lemma \claimref{singularity.schmidt-forcing-proved-outright}'s eigenvector argument fails and the Schmidt basis need not be the number basis, so the reduction need not be diagonal in $N$ and then is not a Gibbs state of $K$ (take $\Omega = c\,|{+}\rangle|0\rangle + s\,|{-}\rangle|1\rangle$ with $|{\pm}\rangle = (|0\rangle \pm |1\rangle)/\sqrt2$ and $c \neq s$, cyclic and separating, whose reduction $\tfrac12\begin{psmallmatrix} 1 & c^{2} - s^{2} \\ c^{2} - s^{2} & 1\end{psmallmatrix}$ has nonzero coherence); but the converse fails, since $\Omega = c|01\rangle + s|10\rangle$ with $cs \neq 0$ is pure, cyclic and separating and not a $G$-eigenvector, yet reduces to $\operatorname{diag}(c^{2}, s^{2})$, Fermi-Dirac at exactly $\TH$ when $s^{2}/c^{2} = e^{-\omega/\TH}$. If (iii) fails, one Schmidt coefficient vanishes and the reduction is pure, not thermal at any finite temperature. The script checks both examples. In general, conditions (i)-(iii) are the hypotheses of Tomita-Takesaki theory, and the identification of modular flow with the boost for horizon-localised algebras is the Bisognano-Wichmann-Sewell mechanism \cite{BW1976, Sewell1982}; the chain's contribution is that, within the class of real rotor flows the geometry supplies, the flow is algebraically \emph{forced} (Theorem \claimref{singularity.modular-structure-completed-pair}(5), with the scope stated there) rather than assumed, and that the single-mode instance is proved outright above rather than quoted.

singularity.modular-structure-completed-.technical:
For a pair $(v, v^*)$ obeying the canonical anticommutation relations, set $\sigma := v^*v - vv^*$. Then $\sigma^2 = 1$, and in the hyperbolic atom $v = \tfrac12(e_0 + e_1)$, $v^* = \tfrac12(e_0 - e_1)$ inside $\Cl(1,1)$ one has $\sigma = e_0e_1$, the unit boost bivector of the plane. The rotor flow $R_\lambda = \exp(\lambda\sigma/2)$ acts by $v \mapsto e^{-\lambda}v$ and $v^* \mapsto e^{\lambda}v^*$, so the pair diagonalises the boost with opposite weights, the structure of outgoing and ingoing horizon modes.

The spectral projectors $\tfrac12(1 \pm \sigma)$ of the boost are exactly the occupation projectors $v^*v$ and $vv^*$, which are the descent projectors, and in the fermionic representation $\sigma = 2N - 1$, so $K := \sigma/2 = N - \tfrac12$. Since $\mathrm{Spin}^+(1,1)$ is one-dimensional, the boost flow is the only one-parameter flow implemented by real rotors of the atom, up to reparametrisation and orientation; this uniqueness holds within real rotor flows of $\Cl(1,1)$, not among all one-parameter unitary groups of $\Mat_2(\C)$.
singularity.modular-structure-completed-.lay: A pair of mutually adjoint elements that each square to zero, like the creation and annihilation operators of a fermion, combines into a single element that behaves as a boost, the geometric operation relating observers in relative motion. This one element plays three roles at once: it generates the boost, it counts whether the mode is occupied, and it produces the two projections later used to discard coherences. Among flows built from real rotations of this small two-dimensional algebra, the boost is the only one, up to its speed and direction.

proofs.main:
(1) $\sigma^2 = (v^*v)^2 + (vv^*)^2 - v^*v\,vv^* - vv^*\,v^*v = v^*v + vv^* - 0 - 0 = 1$, using idempotency (Proposition \claimref{singularity.descent-what-it-erases}) and $v^2 = (v^*)^2 = 0$ to remove the cross terms. In the atom (\claimref{singularity.pseudo-inverse-identities-hyperbolic-atom}): $v v^* = \tfrac14(e_0 + e_1)(e_0 - e_1) = \tfrac14(1 - e_0e_1 + e_1e_0 + 1) = \tfrac12(1 - e_0e_1)$, so $v^*v = 1 - vv^* = \tfrac12(1 + e_0e_1)$ and $\sigma = e_0 e_1$. (2) From $\sigma v = -v$ and $v\sigma = v$ (in the atom: $e_0e_1(e_0 + e_1) = -(e_1 + e_0)$ and $(e_0+e_1)e_0e_1 = e_1 + e_0$; abstractly from $v^2 = (v^*)^2 = 0, \qquad v v^* + v^* v = 1$), and $\sigma^2 = 1$ giving $e^{-\lambda\sigma} = \cosh\lambda - \sigma\sinh\lambda$ (as for any element of square one; in the atom $\sigma = e_0 e_1$ is a bivector with scalar square, the case of \claimref{std-algebra.bivector-exponential}):
\[
e^{\lambda\sigma/2}\,v\,e^{-\lambda\sigma/2} = v\,e^{-\lambda\sigma} = v\cosh\lambda - v\sigma\,\sinh\lambda = (\cosh\lambda - \sinh\lambda)\,v = e^{-\lambda}v ,
\]
using $v\sigma = v$ once; mirror-symmetrically for $v^*$. (3) is $v^*v = \tfrac12(1 + \sigma)$. (4) $N = v^*v$ counts occupation in the two-state module, and $\sigma = 2v^*v - 1$. (5) The even subalgebra of $\Cl(1,1)$ is $\operatorname{span}\{1, \sigma\}$ with $\tilde\sigma = -\sigma$, so the rotors are the elements $a + b\sigma$ with $(a + b\sigma)(a - b\sigma) = a^2 - b^2 = 1$: a one-dimensional group whose tangent line at $1$ is $\R\sigma$. A continuous one-parameter group of rotors is therefore $\lambda \mapsto \exp(c\lambda\sigma/2)$ for a real $c$, which by the closed form (\claimref{std-algebra.bivector-exponential}) is $\cosh\tfrac{c\lambda}{2} + \sigma\sinh\tfrac{c\lambda}{2}$: the boost flow at a rescaled parameter. The rotor group itself has two components, $a \ge 1$ and $a \le -1$; the exponentials fill only the first, and $-1$ is a rotor that is no exponential. A one-parameter flow stays in the identity component, so the uniqueness of (5) is unaffected; it is not the statement that every rotor of the atom is $\exp(\lambda\sigma/2)$.

singularity.modular-theory-matrix-factor.formal:
Let $H = \C^n \otimes \C^n$, let $M = \Mat_n(\C) \otimes 1$ act on the first factor (here the complex numbers are $\C = \mathrm{span}\{1, I_4\}$, the default scalar field of an abstract complex Hilbert space and matrix algebra, and $J$ is the modular conjugation), and let $\Omega = \sum_k \lambda_k\, |kk\rangle$ with all $\lambda_k > 0$ and $\sum \lambda_k^2 = 1$ (any cyclic separating vector of $M$ has this form in its Schmidt basis). Define the Tomita operator as the closure of $S : a\Omega \mapsto a^*\Omega$ ($a \in M$). Then its polar decomposition $S = J\Delta^{1/2}$ has
\[
\Delta = \rho \otimes \bar\rho^{\,-1}, \qquad \rho = \sum_k \lambda_k^2\,|k\rangle\langle k| , \qquad J\,|kl\rangle = |lk\rangle \ \text{(antilinearly)},
\]
and the modular flow on $M$ is $\sigma_t(a) = \rho^{I_4t} a\, \rho^{-I_4t}$. Moreover the state $\omega = \langle\Omega, \cdot\,\Omega\rangle$ satisfies the KMS identity $\omega(ab) = \omega(b\,\rho\,a\,\rho^{-1})$ for all $a, b \in M$.
singularity.modular-theory-matrix-factor.technical:
Take $H = \C^n \otimes \C^n$ over $\C = \mathrm{span}\{1, I_4\}$, $M = \Mat_n(\C) \otimes 1$ and a cyclic separating vector in Schmidt form $\Omega = \sum_k \lambda_k |kk\rangle$ with all $\lambda_k > 0$ and $\sum_k \lambda_k^2 = 1$. The Tomita operator $S : a\Omega \mapsto a^*\Omega$ acts on basis vectors as $|kl\rangle \mapsto (\lambda_k/\lambda_l)|lk\rangle$, and its polar decomposition $S = J\Delta^{1/2}$ is explicit: $\Delta = \rho \otimes \bar\rho^{\,-1}$ with $\rho = \sum_k \lambda_k^2 |k\rangle\langle k|$, and $J$ the antilinear swap $|kl\rangle \mapsto |lk\rangle$.

Consequently the modular flow on $M$ is $\sigma_t(a) = \rho^{I_4t} a \rho^{-I_4t}$, and the vector state $\omega = \langle\Omega, \cdot\,\Omega\rangle$ satisfies the KMS identity $\omega(ab) = \omega(b\,\rho a \rho^{-1})$ for all $a, b \in M$. Because everything is finite-dimensional, all of this follows by direct computation.
singularity.modular-theory-matrix-factor.lay: Tomita-Takesaki theory attaches to a quantum state a natural time evolution, called the modular flow. For two finite quantum systems in an entangled state, this lemma works out every ingredient of that theory by hand. The modular flow turns out to be the evolution generated by the reduced density matrix of one side, and the state satisfies the equilibrium (KMS) condition with respect to it.

proofs.main: Everything is finite-dimensional, so closures are automatic. On the matrix units $a = |k\rangle\langle l| \otimes 1$: $a\Omega = \lambda_l |kl\rangle$ and $a^*\Omega = \lambda_k |lk\rangle$, so $S$ is the antilinear map $|kl\rangle \mapsto (\lambda_k/\lambda_l)\,|lk\rangle$, and since the $a\Omega$ span $H$ ($\Omega$ is cyclic), this determines $S$. Define $\Delta |kl\rangle := (\lambda_k^2/\lambda_l^2)|kl\rangle$, which is exactly $(\rho \otimes \bar\rho^{\,-1})|kl\rangle$, positive and invertible, and let $J$ be the antilinear extension of $|kl\rangle \mapsto |lk\rangle$, which is antiunitary with $J^2 = 1$. Then $J\Delta^{1/2}|kl\rangle = (\lambda_k/\lambda_l) J|kl\rangle = (\lambda_k/\lambda_l)|lk\rangle = S|kl\rangle$ (the eigenvalues are real, so antilinearity causes no conjugation), and uniqueness of the polar decomposition gives the claim. The flow: $\Delta^{I_4t}(b \otimes 1)\Delta^{-I_4t} = (\rho^{I_4t}\otimes\bar\rho^{-I_4t})(b \otimes 1)(\rho^{-I_4t}\otimes\bar\rho^{\,I_4t}) = \rho^{I_4t} b \rho^{-I_4t} \otimes 1$, interior to $M$. KMS: the reduced density matrix of $\Omega$ on the first factor is $\rho$, so $\omega(x) = \tr(\rho x)$ for $x \in \Mat_n(\C)$, and $\omega(b\,\rho a \rho^{-1}) = \tr(\rho\, b\, \rho a \rho^{-1}) = \tr(\rho\, a b) = \omega(ab)$ by cyclicity of the trace.

singularity.net-assembly-net-it-everythi.formal: For $F$ with at least two points, $J(F)$ is the whole $F$-mode algebra, so the two-level discrepancy computed against it vanishes identically. The assignment $F \mapsto J(F)$ is covariant (isotone) under inclusion: it is a net of algebras, the structure of an algebra of regions, and not a presheaf; it has no restriction maps, and the question whether it is a sheaf does not arise. Its ``stalk'' at a point, the algebra generated by the big fibre at $x$ alone, contains elements odd at every other point of $F$.
singularity.net-assembly-net-it-everythi.technical:
For a finite truncation $F = \{x_1, \dots, x_N\}$ of $E$, the net assembly $J(F)$ is the subalgebra of the $F$-mode algebra generated by the big fibres $B_j = \operatorname{Fix}(\operatorname{Ad}\sigma(x_j))$, the elements even in mode $j$. In a Jordan-Wigner representation $\operatorname{Ad}(\sigma_x)$ fixes the ladder $v_y$ for every $y \neq x$, so when $F$ has at least two points every generator of every mode lies in some other point's big fibre, $J(F)$ is the whole $F$-mode algebra, and the two-level discrepancy computed against it vanishes identically.

The assignment $F \mapsto J(F)$ is isotone under inclusion: it is a net of algebras, an algebra of regions, not a presheaf, so it has no restriction maps and the sheaf question does not arise. The algebra generated by the big fibre at a single point $x$ already contains elements, such as $v_y$ for $y \neq x$, that are odd at another point of $F$.
singularity.net-assembly-net-it-everythi.lay: There are two natural ways to build what the classical level can see over a region from what it sees at each point. This result treats the second way, which collects what each point's reading leaves untouched and lets those pieces generate an algebra. With two or more points that algebra is everything, so on this reading the gap between the two levels is zero. The construction behaves like the algebras of regions used in quantum field theory, not like a sheaf.

singularity.p-reduced-metric-level-readi.formal: The mode-wise descents commute, each is the unique conditional expectation of the boundary mode space onto the $\operatorname{Ad}(\sigma_k)$-fixed subalgebra (the elements even in mode $k$, of dimension $4^{N}/2$ on $N$ modes, not the two-dimensional even part of the mode factor alone), and their composite, in any order, is $\EN$: a conditional expectation onto the intersection of the mode-wise ranges, the joint-number-diagonal algebra. Consequently, if the metric-level reading of the full boundary mode space is taken to be the simultaneous performance of the pointwise descents that the localisation attaches, one per point of $E$ (Fact \claimref{singularity.imported-one-sided-completion-singularity}), then that reading is $\EN$ and the metric level is the joint-diagonal algebra, strictly smaller than the total-parity-even algebra on two or more modes. The antecedent is a \emph{choice}, not a consequence: it adopts the sheaf assembly of the pointwise levels over the net assembly, the two quantified, and not decided between, in the section “The metric-level sheaf, and the hopping exclusion”.
singularity.p-reduced-metric-level-readi.technical:
On $N$ completed modes each mode-wise descent $E_k(x) = \tfrac12(x + \sigma_k x \sigma_k)$ is the unique conditional expectation of the whole boundary mode space onto the elements even in mode $k$, a subalgebra of dimension $4^{N}/2$. The $\sigma_k$ are single-site in a Jordan-Wigner representation and commute, so the $E_k$ commute, and their composite in any order is the pinching $\EN$, a conditional expectation onto the intersection of their ranges, the joint-number-diagonal algebra.

Consequently, if the metric-level reading of the boundary mode space is taken to be the simultaneous performance of the pointwise descents that the localisation attaches to the points of $E$, that reading is $\EN$ and the metric level is the joint-diagonal algebra, strictly smaller than the total-parity-even algebra when $N \geq 2$. The antecedent is a choice, the sheaf assembly of the pointwise levels over the net assembly, and is not derived.
singularity.p-reduced-metric-level-readi.lay: When many boundary modes are read at the classical level, the separate one-mode readings can be done in any order and together amount to keeping only the joint occupation records. If one adopts the reading in which every point's own descent is applied, the classical level is exactly that record algebra, which, on two or more modes, is smaller than what fermion parity alone would allow. Adopting that reading is a choice the paper names, not something it proves.

proofs.main: Each $E_k(x) = \tfrac12(x + \sigma_k x \sigma_k)$ is a conditional expectation onto the $\operatorname{Ad}(\sigma_k)$-fixed subalgebra. The automorphism is inner and local, which is what removes any graded-tensor subtlety from the argument: in a Jordan-Wigner representation the string factors of $v_k$ and $v_k^{*}$ cancel in the product $\sigma_k = v_k^{*}v_k - v_k v_k^{*}$, which is single-site, so the fermionic mode-$k$ grading coincides with the spin-picture one and $\operatorname{Ad}(\sigma_k)$ is an automorphism of the full mode algebra. The uniqueness argument of Theorem \claimref{singularity.descent-parity-average} runs verbatim on the full mode algebra: a conditional expectation $F$ onto that subalgebra satisfies $\sigma_k F(x)\sigma_k = F(\sigma_k x \sigma_k)$ by bimodularity ($\sigma_k$ lying in the range), so $F$ annihilates the $\operatorname{Ad}(\sigma_k)$-anti-fixed part and equals $E_k$ on the direct sum. The $\sigma_k$ commute, so the $E_k$ commute; their composite in any order is the group average over $\mathbb{Z}_2^{N}$, which is the pinching $\EN$ of Definition \claimref{obj.singularity.multi-mode-descent}; and the range of a composite of commuting conditional expectations is the intersection of the ranges: an element fixed by every $\operatorname{Ad}(\sigma_k)$ is diagonal in the joint number basis, and conversely. Strict containment for two or more modes is witnessed by elements of the kind $(v_{R_1} + v_{R_1}^{*})(v_{L_1} + v_{L_1}^{*})\,\sigma_{L_2}$ (two Majorana elements and a parity section; in qubit notation $X_{R_1}X_{L_1}Z_{L_2}$, up to the Jordan-Wigner sign string), total-parity even and not joint-diagonal. The script verifies the commutation, the composite-equals-pinching identity, and the idempotence, on generic rational data. The consequence clause takes the modes $k$ to be the ladder pairs that \claimref{singularity.imported-one-sided-completion-singularity} localises, one per point of $E$.

singularity.p-univalence.formal: Physical states of the boundary modes are even: $\omega \circ \alpha = \omega$, equivalently $\omega$ annihilates the odd sector $\Aod$.
singularity.p-univalence.technical:
The premise (P) requires every physical state $\omega$ of the boundary modes to be even under the grading automorphism $\alpha$, that is $\omega \circ \alpha = \omega$. Equivalently, $\omega$ vanishes on the odd sector $\Aod$, so odd elements of the boundary-mode algebra have zero expectation value.

It is a premise, not a derived result: it restricts which states count as physical, and enters as an input wherever it is invoked.
singularity.p-univalence.lay: This is an assumption, not a theorem. It says that the physical states of the modes living on the boundary give zero average to every quantity that changes fermion number by an odd amount. So expectation values never mix the even and odd parity sectors.

singularity.pinching-against-partial-tra.technical:
(i) For one mode, if the global state's Schmidt basis across the pair/partner cut is the number basis, the marginal $\tr_{\mathrm{partner}}\,\rho$ is diagonal in the number basis and hence a fixed point of the pinching $E$: partial trace and pinching coincide, mode by mode.

(ii) On $N \geq 2$ modes, $\tr_L$ and $\EN$ are different maps. They agree on every single-mode marginal, but $\tr_L$ keeps the radiation's off-diagonal joint-number matrix elements while $\EN$ annihilates them, so they differ by exactly the inter-mode coherence. Conflating them is harmless for single-mode spectra and fatal for the computation of correlations.
singularity.pinching-against-partial-tra.lay: There are two ways of looking at one side of an entangled system: forget the partner, or read the system at the classical level. For a single mode, provided the state's entanglement with its partner is lined up with the occupation numbers (its Schmidt basis is the number basis), the two give the same answer. For several modes they differ: forgetting the partner keeps the coherences between modes, while the classical reading erases them. Agreement seen one mode at a time therefore says nothing about correlations.
singularity.pinching-against-partial-tra.typing_note: Removed the mechanical transport-algorithm edge as the proof rests only on the single-mode descent display and the two exact model computations; the Schmidt-forcing and parity-protection lemmas are cited as instances where the clause (i) hypothesis holds, not as premises, so they were not added. (ii) Definition \claimref{obj.singularity.multi-mode-descent}: any state with a nonzero joint-number coherence separates the two maps; the minimal instance, a two-pair state whose pair marginal carries the coherence $c_1 s_1 \gamma$, is computed exactly in Proposition \claimref{singularity.purity-correlation-transfer-recovery}, and its descent, which annihilates that coherence while fixing both populations and both single-mode marginals, is computed exactly in Proposition \claimref{singularity.two-levels-finite-model}. singularity.purity-output-partner-commut.formal: Let $\omega$ be a faithful state on the mode factor (scalars $\mathrm{span}\{1, e_{2}e_{3}\}$, the complex unit of the radial atom, \claimref{synthesis.transverse-bivector-is-the-complex-unit-of-the-radial-atom}; below, $J$ is the modular conjugation of Lemma \claimref{singularity.modular-theory-matrix-factor-proved-outright}, not that unit) with $\varrho = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_0^{2}, \lambda_1^{2})$, $\lambda_i > 0$. In its GNS representation: the space is $\C^{2}\otimes\C^{2}$ and the cyclic vector is $\Omega = \sum_i \lambda_i|ii\rangle$, cyclic and separating for $\pi(\Aa) = \Aa\otimes 1$; the commutant $\pi(\Aa)' = 1 \otimes \Aa$ is the partner copy and equals $J\pi(\Aa)J$; any two purifications of $\omega$ differ by a unitary on the purifying factor alone; and when $\omega$ is the Gibbs state at $\beta$, $\Omega$ is the thermofield double with $\tan\theta = e^{-\omega_k/2T}$, which is exactly the vector Lemma \claimref{singularity.schmidt-forcing-proved-outright} produces. Hypothesis (i) of Theorem \claimref{singularity.modular-descent}, the existence of the partner, and the thermofield form are therefore consequences of the one-sided state rather than independent choices.
singularity.purity-output-partner-commut.technical:
Let $\omega$ be a faithful state on the mode factor with $\varrho = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_0^2, \lambda_1^2)$, $\lambda_i > 0$. Its GNS representation lives on $\C^2 \otimes \C^2$ with cyclic vector $\Omega = \sum_i \lambda_i |ii\rangle$, cyclic and separating for $\pi(\Aa) = \Aa \otimes 1$; the commutant $\pi(\Aa)' = 1 \otimes \Aa = J\pi(\Aa)J$ is the partner copy, and any two purifications of $\omega$ differ by a unitary on the purifying factor alone.

When $\omega$ is the Gibbs state at inverse temperature $\beta$, $\Omega$ is the thermofield double with $\tan\theta = \lambda_1/\lambda_0 = e^{-\omega_k/2T}$, the same vector the Schmidt-forcing argument produces. So purity of the doubled state, the existence of the partner and the thermofield form are consequences of the one-sided state rather than independent choices.
singularity.purity-output-partner-commut.lay: Starting from a single quantum mode in a mixed state, there is a standard construction that builds a larger system in which that state is one half of a pure entangled state. This result shows that the partner needed for the pure state is not an extra ingredient: it emerges automatically as the mirror copy of the mode's own algebra, and the construction is unique up to changes made on the partner side alone. For a thermal state the resulting pure state is the familiar thermofield double.

For the fourth, substituting $\varrho = \operatorname{diag}(1, e^{-\omega_k/T})/Z$ gives $\lambda_1/\lambda_0 = e^{-\omega_k/2T} = \tan\theta$. The script instantiates the purification, the modular eigenvalues and the angle at the rational triple $(\tfrac35, \tfrac45)$.

singularity.schmidt-forcing-proved-outri.formal:
Realise the boost on the doubled system by the one-parameter unitary group $e^{J t G}$, with the scalars of the doubled mode $\mathrm{span}\{1, J\}$, $J = e_{2}e_{3}$ the complex unit of the atom (\claimref{synthesis.transverse-bivector-is-the-complex-unit-of-the-radial-atom}), on both factors, $G = N \otimes 1 - 1 \otimes N$ (the pair carries the flow of Theorem \claimref{singularity.modular-structure-completed-pair}, the partner the mirrored flow). If a unit vector $\Omega \in \C^2 \otimes \C^2$ is invariant up to phase under this group and is cyclic and separating for the pair factor, then
\[
\Omega \;=\; \cos\theta\,|00\rangle + \sin\theta\,|11\rangle \qquad \text{with } \cos\theta\sin\theta \neq 0 ,
\]
up to a global phase and a phase convention on $|11\rangle$: the Schmidt basis is the number basis.
singularity.schmidt-forcing-proved-outri.technical:
Let the boost act on the doubled mode $\C^2 \otimes \C^2$, with scalars $\mathrm{span}\{1, J\}$ ($J = e_2e_3$, the atom's complex unit), by the unitary group $e^{JtG}$ with $G = N \otimes 1 - 1 \otimes N$. If a unit vector $\Omega$ is invariant up to phase under this group and is cyclic and separating for the pair factor, then up to a global phase and a phase convention on $|11\rangle$, $\Omega = \cos\theta\,|00\rangle + \sin\theta\,|11\rangle$ with $\cos\theta\sin\theta \neq 0$.

Invariance up to phase makes $\Omega$ an eigenvector of $G$, which acts as $G|jk\rangle = (j - k)|jk\rangle$. The eigenvectors for $\pm 1$ are product vectors, which cannot be cyclic and separating, so $\Omega$ lies in the zero eigenspace spanned by $|00\rangle$ and $|11\rangle$, and both coefficients must be nonzero for the same reason. The Schmidt basis is therefore the number basis.
singularity.schmidt-forcing-proved-outri.lay: Take one mode together with its partner. If their joint state is unchanged by the boost, apart from an overall phase, and is genuinely entangled, then there is no freedom in which basis the entanglement uses: it must pair empty with empty and occupied with occupied. Only the balance between those two terms is left free.
singularity.schmidt-forcing-proved-outri.typing_note: Removed the mechanical transport-algorithm edge: the proof is a spectral computation on the explicit generator G; the modular structure theorem is cited only to name G as the boost and was not added, so this lemma now has no premises. Levels pass: conditions already kept.

proofs.main: Invariance up to phase under a one-parameter unitary group means $\Omega$ is an eigenvector of its generator. $G$ is diagonal in the product number basis with $G|jk\rangle = (j - k)|jk\rangle$: eigenvalue $0$ on $\operatorname{span}\{|00\rangle, |11\rangle\}$, eigenvalue $+1$ on $\C|10\rangle$, eigenvalue $-1$ on $\C|01\rangle$. An eigenvector for $\pm 1$ is a product vector, and a product vector is annihilated by some nonzero $a \in M$ (respectively fails cyclicity), contradicting separating; so $\Omega = c_0|00\rangle + c_1|11\rangle$. If either coefficient vanished, $\Omega$ would again be a product vector; so both are nonzero, and phases can be absorbed into the basis vectors, leaving the stated real form.

singularity.sheaf-assembly-sheaf.formal: $\mathfrak{M}$ is a sheaf of algebras on $E$, with stalk at $x$ the germs valued in $\Aa_x^{+}$. It exists whenever the completed mode bundle $\Aa$ does, that is under the standing hypothesis $w_1(\shL) = 0$, and needs nothing further: the fibrewise projection $\tfrac12(\id + \alpha_x)$ is a smooth idempotent bundle map, so $\Aa^{+}$ is a locally trivial subbundle, and it is defined by $\sigma$, which does not see the sign of the ladder. For $w_1(\shL) \neq 0$ the mode bundle itself exists only in the $\shL$-twisted variant; its even part, $\mathrm{span}\{1, \sigma\}$, is untwisted, so $\mathfrak{M}$ is defined there as well and does not see the twist (Proposition \claimref{three-routes.it-sheaf-risk-resolves-into-standing}).
singularity.sheaf-assembly-sheaf.technical:
Given the completed mode bundle $\Aa$ over $E$, with parity section $\sigma$ and fibre automorphism $\alpha_x = \operatorname{Ad}(\sigma(x))$, the sheaf assembly $\mathfrak{M}(U) = \Gamma(U, \Aa^{+})$ assigns to each open $U \subseteq E$ the sections valued in the even fibres $\Aa_x^{+} = \operatorname{span}\{1, \sigma(x)\}$. Because $\tfrac12(\id + \alpha_x)$ is a smooth idempotent bundle map, $\Aa^{+}$ is a locally trivial subbundle, and $\mathfrak{M}$ is a sheaf of algebras with stalk at $x$ the germs valued in $\Aa_x^{+}$.

It exists whenever $\Aa$ does, that is under the standing hypothesis $w_1(\shL) = 0$, and needs nothing further, since $\sigma$ is quadratic in the ladder and does not see its sign. For $w_1(\shL) \neq 0$ the mode bundle exists only in the $\shL$-twisted variant; its even part is untwisted, so $\mathfrak{M}$ is defined there as well and does not see the twist.
singularity.sheaf-assembly-sheaf.lay: One way to assemble the classical level over a region is to keep, at each point, only the part that survives that point's descent, and glue those parts together. This result checks that the gluing really does give a sheaf, the standard mathematical structure for locally defined data. It needs nothing beyond the existence of the bundle of completed modes, which holds under the paper's standing topological hypothesis.
singularity.sheaf-assembly-sheaf.typing_note: Kept the one-sided completion fact as the premise that supplies the mode bundle under w1 = 0; added the two-assemblies definition as the object the statement is about, with a version bump for the new about edge. Levels pass: conditions already kept.

proofs.main: Sections of a vector bundle form a sheaf: locality and gluing are inherited from the sections of $\Aa$, membership being a fibrewise condition, and restriction is restriction of sections. Multiplication is fibrewise and preserves evenness. The subbundle statement is the idempotent, smooth because $\sigma$ is a smooth section; the stalk is then as stated. The $w_1$ clause is Fact \claimref{singularity.imported-one-sided-completion-singularity}'s standing hypothesis, which is what puts $\Aa$ in place; that the rest is sign-insensitive is the quadratic dependence of $\sigma$ on the ladder, $\sigma \mapsto \sigma$ under $(k, k^{*}) \mapsto (-k, -k^{*})$.

singularity.two-kms-functionals-sign.technical:
On the mode factor, over the atom's complex unit $J = e_2e_3$, with flow $\alpha_t = \operatorname{Ad}(e^{Jt\omega K})$ and fermion parity $\Gamma = 1 - 2N$, fix $\beta > 0$. The functionals satisfying the ungraded KMS identity $\phi(ab) = \phi(b\,\alpha_{J\beta}(a))$ are the multiples of $\tr(e^{-\beta\omega K}\,\cdot\,)$; normalised, this is the unique KMS state, with $Z = 1 + e^{-\beta\omega}$ and occupancy $(e^{\beta\omega} + 1)^{-1}$. The functionals satisfying the graded identity, with a sign $\epsilon_b = -1$ for odd $b$, are the multiples of $\tr(\Gamma e^{-\beta\omega K}\,\cdot\,)$, with $Z_\Gamma = 1 - e^{-\beta\omega}$ and negative occupancy, so this functional is not a state.

The $+1$ of the Fermi-Dirac denominator is therefore the $+$ sign between the two module states in $Z$. The gluing condition of (R), which reverses the order of $a$ and $b$ without a sign, is the ungraded identity, and it selects the state.
singularity.two-kms-functionals-sign.lay: For a single fermionic mode there are two versions of the equilibrium condition, differing by a sign for odd operators. The version without the sign gives the genuine thermal state, with the familiar Fermi-Dirac occupation. The version with the sign gives something with a negative occupation, which is not a physical state at all. The plus sign in the Fermi-Dirac formula comes from this choice, and the paper's regularity condition picks the version without the sign.
singularity.two-kms-functionals-sign.typing_note: Removed the mechanical transport-algorithm edge since the proof is KMS uniqueness plus a trace computation on the mode factor; the Fermi-Dirac and Matsubara statements the paper calls standard have no imported claim in the store, so no standard-route derivation was added.

proofs.main: (1) is Theorem \claimref{singularity.kms-uniqueness-factor}, read over the atom's scalars $\mathrm{span}\{1, J\}$ (its unit $I_4$ there standing for the factor's scalar unit, here $J$), with $K$ replaced by $\omega K$, and $Z = \tr e^{-\beta\omega K} = e^{\beta\omega/2}(1 + e^{-\beta\omega})$, the prefactor cancelling in the normalised state. (2) Write $\phi = \tr(\varrho\,\cdot\,)$ and $H := \omega K$. The graded identity with $b$ homogeneous is $\tr(b\varrho a) = \epsilon_b\tr(e^{\beta H}\varrho\,b\,e^{-\beta H}a)$ for all $a$, i.e.\ $b\,(\varrho e^{\beta H}) = \epsilon_b\,(e^{\beta H}\varrho)\,b$. With $b = 1$: $\varrho$ commutes with $e^{\beta H}$, hence with $H$, hence is diagonal. Then $c := \varrho e^{\beta H}$ is diagonal, commutes with the even elements and anticommutes with $v$ and $v^{*}$; for $c = \operatorname{diag}(c_0, c_1)$ the relation $cv = -vc$ reads $c_0 = -c_1$, so $c \propto \Gamma$ and $\varrho \propto \Gamma e^{-\beta H}$. Conversely $\Gamma e^{-\beta H}$ satisfies the graded identity because $\Gamma$ commutes with $H$ and $b\Gamma = \epsilon_b\Gamma b$. Its trace is $e^{\beta\omega/2}(1 - e^{-\beta\omega})$ and $\tr(\Gamma e^{-\beta H}N) = -e^{-\beta\omega}e^{\beta\omega/2}$, giving the displayed ratio. (3) is read off (1) and (2): $\tr(e^{-\beta H}) $ and $\tr(\Gamma e^{-\beta H})$ differ exactly in the sign of the occupied term. state-selection.imported-general-stateme.formal: For a $C^{*}$-dynamical system the $(\alpha,\beta)$-KMS states at fixed $\beta$ form a weak$^{*}$-compact convex simplex whose extreme points are exactly those whose GNS von Neumann algebra is a factor, distinct extremal KMS states being disjoint; in particular a factor state is extremal, and uniqueness of the $\beta$-KMS state is the statement that the simplex is a point. \emph{Provenance:} Bratteli and Robinson \cite[Thm.~5.3.30]{BR2}; the KMS condition itself is Haag, Hugenholtz and Winnink \cite{HHW1967}. The companion statement that two faithful normal states have the same modular automorphism group only if they differ by an element affiliated to the centre is Connes' Radon-Nikodym cocycle theorem \cite[Thm.~1.2.1]{Connes1973}, which for a factor forces the two states to be equal.
state-selection.imported-general-stateme.technical:
For a $C^{*}$-dynamical system, the $(\alpha, \beta)$-KMS states at fixed $\beta$ form a weak$^{*}$-compact convex simplex whose extreme points are exactly the states whose GNS von Neumann algebra is a factor; distinct extremal KMS states are disjoint, a factor state is extremal, and uniqueness of the $\beta$-KMS state is the statement that the simplex is a single point. This is Bratteli and Robinson's theorem, with the KMS condition itself due to Haag, Hugenholtz and Winnink.

The companion result is Connes' Radon-Nikodym cocycle theorem: two faithful normal states with the same modular automorphism group differ by an element affiliated to the centre, which on a factor forces them to be equal.
state-selection.imported-general-stateme.lay: This is a standard result from the mathematics of quantum statistical mechanics. At a fixed temperature the possible equilibrium states form a well-behaved convex set, and its extreme points, the pure thermodynamic phases, are exactly the states whose algebra has trivial centre. A related theorem of Connes says that on such an algebra a faithful state is determined by its own modular time evolution.

imported_from.citation: O. Bratteli and D. W. Robinson, Operator Algebras and Quantum Statistical Mechanics 2: Equilibrium States. Models in Quantum Statistical Mechanics, 2nd ed., Springer (1997).

A. Connes, Une classification des facteurs de type III, Ann. Sci. 'Ec. Norm. Sup'er. (4) 6 (1973), 133--252.

state-selection.partner-purification-are.technical:
For a faithful state $\omega$ on $\Aa \cong \Mat_2(\C)$ with $\rho = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_0^{2}, \lambda_1^{2})$, the GNS representation is $\C^2 \otimes \C^2$ with vector $\Omega = \sum_i \lambda_i |ii\rangle$, cyclic and separating for $\pi(\Aa) = \Aa \otimes 1$. The commutant $1 \otimes \Aa = J\pi(\Aa)J$ is the partner copy, and any two purifications of $\omega$ differ by a unitary on the purifying factor, so $\Omega$ is unique up to a unitary in the commutant.

For the Gibbs state, $\lambda_0 = \cos\theta$ and $\lambda_1 = \sin\theta$ with $\tan\theta = e^{-\omega_k/2T}$, so $\Omega$ is the thermofield double. Global purity, the partner and the thermofield form are thus consequences of the one-sided state, and the two ends of the pair are the algebra and its commutant in the state's own GNS representation.
state-selection.partner-purification-are.lay: Given only the state of one mode, a standard construction builds a larger pure state in which that mode is entangled with a partner. The partner turns out to be the mirror image of the mode's own algebra, and the construction is unique up to changes made on the partner side. For a thermal mode the result is the thermofield double, so purity and the partner do not have to be assumed separately.
